Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper
Electroplating Applications of Microvia
Zewei Lin<sup>1,2</sup> · Zhihua Tao<sup>1</sup> · Yuxuan Huang<sup>1</sup> · Jihua Zhang<sup>2,3</sup>
Accepted: 5 May 2025 / Published online: 17 May 2025
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025
Abstract
Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically
studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling. The synergistic efects
between TW and other additives were verified by means of chronopotentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemi-
cal impedance spectroscopy. The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior
between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection.
Metallographic section analysis demonstrated that TW exhibits outstanding microvia filling capabilities for micro blind
vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm. Notably, TW-80 was able to attain a filling rate of 96.15% following
electrodeposition for 60 min at a current density of 2 A/dm<sup>2</sup>. Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively
smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode
surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.
Keywords Tween · Suppressor · Copper electroplating · Microvia filling

Electrochemical Details
The electrochemical measurements were performed with a
CHI760E (ChenHua) electrochemical workstation, which
was furnished with the conventional three electrodes and a
100 mL three-electrode cell capable of accommodating an
virgin makeup solution (VMS) of 220 g/L CuSO4·5H2O
and 28.33 mL/L H2SO4. A platinum rotating disk elec-
trode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm was employed as
the working electrode, while a copper strip with a diameter
of 4 mm served as the counter electrode. The experiment

erence electrode. To evaluate the electroplating efects of

Cross Section Analysis of OM
The PCB test panels had a thickness of 1 mm, with a via
diameter ranging from 120 to 150 µm and a via depth of
75 µm. Electroplating processes were conducted in a har-
ing cell with a capacity of 1.5 L and the electroplating
solution maintained a flow rate of 2.0 L per minute. The
area of the cathode test plate immersed in the electroplat-
ing solution measures 50 mm × 60 mm, while the total
area of the test plate is approximately 80 mm × 60 mm.
In order to enhance the electrical conductivity between
the copper plating and the Cu seed layer, the test boards
underwent a series of decontamination processes before
plating. The specific operational procedure is as follows:
acid cleaning agent followed by deionized water rinse,
micro-etching, another deionized water rinse, acid dip-
ping, and finally copper electroplating in an acid bath. The
electroplating test was conducted at ambient temperature
with the current density maintained at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0
A/dm2 for various plating durations. Continuous agita-
tion was achieved by stirring the solution with flowing
air bubbles to ensure thorough mixing of the plating solu-
tion and facilitate efective mass transfer in the plating
cell. The composition of the plating solution included 220
g/L CuSO4·5H2O, 28.33 mL/L H2SO4, 100 mg/L TW,
6 mg/L bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), 60 mg/L Cl-
and 8 mg/L 1-(4-Hydroxyphenyl)−1H-tetrazole-5-thiol
(HPTT). The filling rate (F) of microvias is defined by
F = \frac {A}{B} \times 100\tag{2}
where A is the depth of the copper filled in the blind via; B is
the distance from the bottom of the via to the surface of the
filled copper as illustrated in Fig. 2, and C is the electroplat-
ing copper thickness on the surface of PCBs [28].
Calculation Methods
The molecular structures of TW-20 and TW-80 were opti-
mized using the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) method with Gauss-
ian09 W software. The optimization of Tween's molecu-
lar structure was conducted based on frontier molecular
orbital theory, focusing on the lowest unoccupied molecu-
lar orbital (LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular
orbital (HOMO) [29]. The forcite module and VMD soft-
ware were respectively adopted to investigate the interac-
tion between copper surface and Tween and visualize the
optimized geometry and molecular orbitals [30]. Tween
molecular dynamics properties in the aqueous phase such
as radius of gyration, radial distribution function and dif-
fusion coeficient were investigated by the Material Studio
software at the temperature of 298 K. The COMPASSII
force field was utilized to optimize the size and simulate
the adsorption process of Tween.
Results and Discussion
Electrochemical Evaluation
The study investigated the inhibitory efects of TW and iden-
tified the optimal concentration that exhibited the highest
inhibitory strength, as depicted in Fig. 3. It can be observed
that when there is no Cl- and TW, the anode peak current
density is the highest, reaching 15.69 A/dm<sup>2</sup>and 18.82 A/
dm<sup>2</sup>respectively. When Cl- and TW are added, the lowest val-
ues of the anode peak current density are 6.35 A/dm<sup>2</sup>and 4.95
A/dm<sup>2</sup>respectively. Meanwhile, the polarization potential of
copper deposition obviously shifts in the negative direction.

Under the condition of a current density of 2 A/dm<sup>2</sup>, the cor-
responding deposition potentials are −0.666 V and −0.678 V
respectively. During the forward scanning process, the disso-
lution peak of copper decreases significantly. Table 1 lists the
values of the integral area Q of the copper dissolution peak
on the CV curve measured in the electroplating solutions
containing inhibitors with diferent concentrations.
In general, a lower Q value signifies a more potent inhibi-
tory efect of the inhibitor. These outcomes suggest that as the
concentration of inhibitors increase, both TW-20 and TW-80
reach their maximum inhibitory strength at a concentration of
100–200 mg/L. Additionally, within the concentration range of
50–200 mg/L, TW-80 demonstrates a superior inhibitory efect
compared to TW-20. The findings of this experiment align
with previous research [31], which demonstrates that inhibi-
tors with larger molecular weights exhibit stronger inhibitory
capabilities when their molecular structures are consistent.
Following the determination of the inhibitory strengths of
the two inhibitors, this study utilized the chronopotentiom-
etry to predict the hole-filling capacity of the plating solu-
tion consisting of 60 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L accelerator, 4 mg/L
HPTT and separate batches of 200 mg/L TW-20 or TW-80.
The test results are shown in Fig. 4. The analysis of the test
results indicated that the plating solutions containing distinct
inhibitors all adhered to the convection-dependent adsorption
(CDA) of additives [32], as evidenced by a notable negative
shift in the stable potential measured at high rotation speeds.
In other words, the inhibitors exhibit a stronger inhibitory
efect under conditions of strong convection, thereby com-
plicating the process of copper deposition. Furthermore, it
can be inferred from Fig. 4 that the overpotential for copper
deposition with TW-80 is higher than that with TW-20, which
remains unafected by the intensity of convection. After com-
paring the potential diference Δη calculated for the two inhib-
itors at diferent rotation speeds, it becomes apparent that Δη
for TW-80 consistently exceeds that for TW-20 at equivalent
concentrations. According to the CDA mechanism, a higher
Δη of the plating solution is associated with increased hole-
filling capability [32], suggesting that TW-80 is expected to
have a more robust capacity for filling holes.
Combining the CV and potential-time images, the optimal
concentration for both TW-20 and TW-80 was determined
to be 100 mg/L. Using the same method, the optimal elec-
troplating formulations corresponding to TW-20 and TW-80
were obtained: (a). 40 mg/L Cl-, 100 mg/L TW-20, 6 mg/L
SPS and 8 mg/L HPTT; (b)0.30 mg/L Cl-, 100 mg/L TW-80,
6 mg/L SPS and 8 mg/L HPTT.

results in the adsorption of TW molecules on the elec-

inhibitory efect on copper ion deposition.

Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco—
friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in micro-
via applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly,
when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydro-
philic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching
structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper
adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration
optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high con-
centrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality,
thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal bal-
ance. Thirdly, using Tween compounds in combination with
other electroplating additives and understanding their syner-
gistic efects can enhance the overall plating performance,
although their compatibility and interaction mechanisms
need thorough investigation. Finally, environmental con-
siderations are essential, including minimizing compound
loss during bath operation and adopting appropriate biodeg-
radation processes for waste treatment. By adhering to these
guidelines, Tween compounds can be efectively applied,
promoting more sustainable and eficient microelectronics
manufacturing, and future research should further explore
and optimize their application.
